title: Adaptive backfill + graceful GPU eviction — prototype playbook
content:
Purpose:
This document is a prototype runbook for performing adaptive backfill and graceful GPU eviction during infra failures that cause capacity loss (failed accelerator, kernel panic, thermal event, or zonal network flaps). The aim is to keep inference SLAs stable while minimizing request failures and avoiding cache-poisoning regressions.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to hosted and dedicated clusters running Redwood serving runtime (k8s-based node pools with GPU instances).
- Assumes autoscaler is enabled for ephemeral backfill pools (label: gpu-backfill=true).
- Customers may be routed to secondary model variants (lower-memory / quantized) when capacity constrained.
- This is a prototype — expect gaps and site-specific knobs.

High-level strategy:
1) Detect early-capacity-loss and enter Safe Mode: prioritize low-latency and critical customers and avoid large-scale preemption.
2) Fast backfill: spin up ephemeral backfill nodes in parallel with graceful evictions on impacted nodes.
3) Preserve KV/prefix cache integrity: avoid killing pods that hold hot KV caches until state replicated/warmed elsewhere.
4) Controlled eviction: drain workloads by priority, with backpressure on new requests and temporary routing rules.
5) Validation & rollforward: confirm request success rates and latency SLA; then mark nodes for replacement or repair.

Runbook quick actions (oncall checklist):
- Pager/alert triage: note time, alert name, impacted zones, and affected model routes.
- Notify: #oncall-sre and #infra-incidents with one-line summary (template below).
- Enter incident channel (create if not present): #incident-<YYYYMMDD>-<short>.
- Snapshot: capture cluster state (kubectl get nodes -o wide, describe failing pods, dmesg from node if accessible).

Immediate commands (safe, read-only):
- kubectl get nodes -l cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool -o wide
- kubectl get pods -A -o wide | grep Evicted
- kubectl describe node <NODE>
- gcloud compute ssh <node> -- zone=<zone> --command='sudo journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager | tail -n 200'
- Request autoscaler status: kubectl get hpa -n infra

Safe Mode entry (automated + manual checks):
- Set routing policy to preserve critical customers: curl -X POST $ROUTER_API/route-policy -d '{"mode":"safe","priority_tiers":["enterprise","critical"]}'
- Set global token-limit throttle: redis patch to limiter config or toggle feature-flag: feature.limit_requests = true
- Reduce batch sizes for generation workers: patch configmap gen-runtime: BATCH_MAX=4

Backfill procedure (preferred order):
1) Start ephemeral backfill pool:
   - Terraform/infra: terraform apply -var='pool_type=backfill' -target=module.gpu_backfill
   - Or: gcloud compute instance-groups managed resize <backfill-igm> --size=<N>
2) Confirm nodes become Ready and GPU drivers present: kubectl get nodes -l gpu-backfill=true -o wide
3) Label nodes as warm-target for cache replication: kubectl label node <node> warm-target=true
4) Trigger KV cache replication: POST /infra/kv/replicate?target=warm-target (or run internal script replicate-kv.sh)
5) Wait for replication metric: infra.kv.replication_complete{target="warm-target"} == 1

Controlled eviction sequence (avoid wholesale pod kills):
- Evict by priority groups (use pod label ownerTier: enterprise|paid|platinum|free):
  1. cordon impacted node: kubectl cordon <node>
  2. for free-tier pods: kubectl delete pod <pod> --grace-period=30 --now=false (allow graceful shutdown)
  3. for paid-tier pods: use kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force --grace-period=120 --pod-selector='ownerTier!=enterprise'
- Monitor pending pods to avoid scheduling storms: kubectl get events -w
- If a pod holds hot KV and is in the drain path, move it to backfill node explicitly: kubectl delete pod <pod> --force=false then patch deployment to nodeSelector: gpu-backfill=true

Machine replacement vs. hot-swap decision guide:
- If node shows transient kernel OOMs, try reboot first: gcloud compute instances reset <node>
- If GPU ECC or hardware flagged by vendor diagnostics, schedule replacement: open hardware ticket and mark node for decommission (label decommission=true).
- If expected repair > 30m, continue backfill and migrate state.

Routing and model fallback knobs:
- Enable lower-memory model variants for burst traffic: POST $ROUTER_API/switch-variant with route prefix and % traffic.
- Automatic fallback policy to quantized variants when queue length > 200 across region.

Observability & validation:
- Dashboards to watch: infra/gpu-utilization, serving/latency-p50-p95-p99, infra/queued-requests, infra/kv-hit-rate
- Key metrics to hit before rollforward:
  - cluster-ready-capacity >= required_capacity * 0.98
  - p95 latency within SLA for enterprise customers
  - error-rate drops below baseline + 0.5% absolute

Communication templates:
- Initial Slack alert (paste to #oncall-sre and #infra-incidents):
  "INCIDENT (investigating): GPU capacity loss in zone-<zone>. Affected routes: /v1/gen, /v1/chat. Entered Safe Mode, starting backfill. Owner: Asha Raman. Jira: SRE-4123"
- Customer-facing one-liner (for CS to use):
  "We are investigating increased inference latency and degraded throughput in <region>. We have activated mitigation steps and will provide updates every 15 minutes."

Post-incident checks and cleanup:
- Confirm all nodes that were cordoned are either replaced or returned to Ready: kubectl get nodes -l decommission!=true
- Remove warm-target labels after TTL (24h) and drain backfill nodes if not needed: kubectl label node <node> warm-target-
- Revert routing safe-mode: POST $ROUTER_API/route-policy -d '{"mode":"normal"}'
- Re-enable batch sizes and caches to pre-incident values, monitor RMSE of outputs for regression.

Postmortem template (quickfields for incident review):
- Incident ID: link to channel + Jira (SRE-4123)
- Timeline: timestamps for detection, Safe Mode entry, backfill start, last node replaced, service return to normal
- Impact: % of requests errored, p99 latency delta, affected customers list
- Root cause hypothesis: hardware / kernel / driver / scheduling storm / autoscaler lag
- Short-term mitigations implemented: safe-mode, backfill count, model-fallback
- Long-term actions (owner + due date): replace node image, adjust autoscaler cooldown, add KV cross-replication, add healthcheck to detect thermal events earlier
- Severity and SLA impact: note any compensations or credits required

Testing checklist (run during non-incident windows):
- Simulate: cordon & drain a mix of nodes with hot-cached pods and verify replication path
- Exercise backfill: spin up backfill pool, warm caches, measure warm-up time and p95 latency impact
- Chaos test: kill 2% of GPU pods across two zones and validate routing fallback works without customer-visible errors

Playbook open items (prototype parity gaps):
- Automated KV replication API is not yet GA; current script is manual and runs on a single operator host. Need a controller.
- Backfill TTL and cost accounting integration into billing signals.
- Fine-grained pod priority labels absent in some legacy stacks — require migration.

Notes to operators / caveats:
- Do not perform mass --force delete on pods with ownerTier=enterprise unless explicitly approved by SRE lead — caches and request ordering can be violated.
- Be cautious with driver reinstallation on live nodes — a kernel-module reload can drop active CUDA contexts and corrupt in-flight state. Prefer cold-replace if possible.

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
- list pods by tier: kubectl get pods -A -l 'ownerTier' -o custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,TIER:.metadata.labels.ownerTier
- cordon + drain with selector: kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --pod-selector='ownerTier!=enterprise' --grace-period=60
- replicate-kv helper (operator host): /opt/sre/bin/replicate-kv.sh --source-node=<node> --target-label=warm-target
- quick health snapshot script (local): /opt/sre/bin/cluster-snapshot.sh --out=/tmp/snapshot-$(date +%s).tgz

Owner note: This is intentionally prescriptive in some steps and intentionally high-level in others — we're prototyping a safe, automated path for low-latency inference clusters that preserves hot-cache integrity. Please add improvements and run the testing checklist before considering this playbook final.

Recent changes log:
